'''Jean Prestet''' (1648–1690) was a French [[Oratory of Jesus|Oratorian]] [[Priesthood (Catholic Church)|priest]] and [[mathematician]] who contributed to the fields of [[combinatorics]]<ref>
{{cite book
  |last=Schneider
  |first=Ivo
  |chapter=Jakob Bernoulli, ''Ars Conjectandi'' (1713)
  |editor-last=Grattan-Guinness
  |editor-first=I.
  |title=Landmark Writings in Mathematics 1640–1940
  |year=2005
  |publisher=Elsevier
  |isbn=0-444-50871-6
  |page=96
}}</ref><ref>{{cite book
  |last = Knobloch
  |first = Eberhard |author-link=Eberhard Knobloch
  |editor-last = Wilson
  |editor-first = Robin |editor-link=Robin Wilson (mathematician)
  |editor-last2 = Watkins
  |editor-first2 = John J.
  |chapter = Renaissance Combinatorics
  |title = Combinatorics: Ancient & Modern
  |pages = 141
  |publisher = Oxford
}}</ref> and [[number theory]].

Prestet grew up poor. As a teenager, he worked as a servant of the [[Oratory of Jesus]] in [[Paris]]. He was promoted to secretary for [[Nicolas Malebranche]], who taught him mathematics.

Under the guidance of Malebranche, Prestet began work in 1670 on the textbook ''Elémens des Mathématiques''.<ref>{{cite book
  |last = Asselah
  |first = Katia
  |title = Arithmétique et algèbre dans la deuxième moitié du XVIIe siècle français : les Elemens et Nouveaux éléments des mathématiques de Jean Prestet
  |year=2005
  |publisher = University Paris VII (Ph D thesis)
}}</ref> Unusually for the time, the textbook focused exclusively on algebra but did not cover geometry at all.<ref name="Schrubing2005">
{{cite book
  |last=Schrubring
  |first=Gert
  |title=Conflicts Between Generalization, Rigor, and Intuition
  |publisher=Springer
  |isbn=0-387-22836-5
  |year=2005
  |page=52
}}</ref> Prestet believed that algebra was the most fundamental field of mathematics, and geometry merely applied algebra.<ref name="Schubring">{{cite book
  |editor-last=Karp
  |editor-first=Alexander
  |editor-last2=Schubring
  |editor-first2=Gert
  |title=Handbook on the History of Mathematics
  |publisher=Springer
  |isbn=978-1-4614-9154-5
  |lccn=2013949144
  |year=2014}}</ref>{{rp|461}} Gert Schubring writes that "[t]he self-confidence of Prestet in claiming superiority for the 'moderns' over the 'ancients' … proved to be a bold and modernizing approach, disseminating [[René Descartes|Cartesian]] conceptions and preparing the way for [[rationalism]] in France."<ref name="Schubring" />{{rp|137}}

The book contained a proof of [[Descartes' rule of signs]] that Prestet later acknowledged to be incomplete.<ref name="scienceseries">
{{citation
  |last=Cajori
  |first=Florian
  |title=A History of the Arithmetical Methods of Approximation to the Roots of Numerical Equations of One Unknown Quantity
  |publisher=Colorado College
  |location=Colorado Springs, Colorado
  |page=186
  |year=1910
}}</ref> It also included a generalization of [[Euclid's lemma]] to non-prime divisors.<ref>
{{cite book
  |author = Euclid
  |authorlink = Euclid
  |title = Les Éléments, traduction, commentaires et notes
  |translator = Bernard Vitrac
  |language = French
  |volume = 2
  |pages = 338–339
}}</ref>

''Elémens'' was published in 1675 by the Oratorian order for use in the curriculum of the many Oratorian colleges. Starting in the early 17th century, the order had founded colleges in smaller cities and towns to challenge the influence of the [[Society of Jesus|Jesuits]]. ''Elémens'' was one of several textbooks published around that time by notable Oratorian mathematics instructors including [[Bernard Lamy]].<ref name="Schubring" />{{rp|137}} [[Abraham de Moivre]] used ''Elémens'' in an abortive early attempt to teach himself mathematics.<ref name="Bellhouse">
{{cite book
  |title=Abraham De Moivre: Setting the Stage for Classical Probability and Its Applications
  |url=https://archive.org/details/abrahamdemoivres00bell_545
  |url-access=limited
  |last=Bellhouse
  |first=David R.
  |publisher=CRC Press
  |year=2011
  |isbn=978-1-56881-349-3
  |page=[https://archive.org/details/abrahamdemoivres00bell_545/page/n19 19]
}}</ref>

With the publication of ''Elémens'', Prestet's reputation as a mathematics instructor grew. He was appointed the mathematical chair at the [[University of Angers]] in 1681. A revised and expanded edition, titled ''Nouveaux Elémens des mathématiques'', was published in 1689.<ref name="Knuth">{{cite book
  |last=Knuth
  |first=Donald
  |authorlink=Donald E. Knuth
  |title=The Art of Computer Programming
  |volume=4 fasicle 4
  |publisher=Pearson
  |year=2006
  |pages=64
  |isbn=0-321-33570-8
  |title-link=The Art of Computer Programming
 }}</ref> This edition included some early work on the [[fundamental theorem of arithmetic]].<ref name="Goldstein" />
